paras.text: In recent years, youth violence has become a serious social concern worldwide. The World Health Organization has identified violence as an important cause of death and injury among young people. Worldwide, approximately 200,000 homicides occur each year among youth and young adults aged 10–29 years (World Health Organization, 2015). Aggressive behavior is an important precursor to and risk factor for youth violence. Previous studies have shown that aggression is associated with mental health problems among adolescents, including depression and anxiety (Li et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024). Higher levels of aggression during childhood and adolescence may also increase the risk of subsequent delinquent and criminal behavior (Huesmann et al., 2002). In China, specialized schools evolved from reform schools and are primarily responsible for providing specialized education and correction to minors who have engaged in serious misconduct. Specialized education is an important protective measure designed to educate and correct minors with serious misconduct, and it differs in nature from criminal punishment. According to the Law of the People’s Republic of China on the Prevention of Juvenile Delinquency, serious misconduct includes acts prescribed by criminal law for which minors are not subject to criminal punishment because they have not reached the age of criminal responsibility, as well as acts that seriously endanger society, such as group fighting, intentional injury, and theft. Students in specialized schools are minors who, following an assessment and formal decision, are placed in these schools to receive specialized education because of such serious misconduct. Comparative research has shown that students in specialized schools exhibit higher levels of aggression than students in regular schools (Li et al., 2017). Among students in specialized schools, aggression may undermine the effectiveness of education and correction and increase the risk that problem behaviors will persist or escalate. Therefore, examining the factors associated with aggression in this population is important for improving education and correction, enhancing the quality of specialized education, and preventing youth violence and delinquency. Adolescence is a critical period marked by rapid development in cognition, self-regulation, and social relationships. When facing negative interpersonal situations such as rejection, some adolescents may respond with aggressive behavior (Quarmley et al., 2023). Aggressive behavior refers to any behavior intended to cause harm or pain to others (Anderson and Bushman, 2002). The General Aggression Model (GAM) provides a systematic theoretical framework for understanding how negative situations are associated with aggressive behavior. According to the GAM, individual and situational factors serve as input variables that influence internal states, including cognition, affect, and physiological arousal. These internal states further shape appraisal and decision-making processes, which may ultimately result in aggressive or nonaggressive behavior (Allen et al., 2018). Social exclusion is a typical negative interpersonal experience and can be viewed as an adverse situational input within the GAM. It refers to experiences of being ignored, rejected, or excluded by others or groups, which may threaten individuals’ needs for belonging and social connection (Rajchert and Winiewski, 2016; Williams, 2009). A meta-analysis of 92 studies with 99 independent samples found a moderate positive association between social exclusion and aggressive behavior, indicating that individuals who experience greater social exclusion tend to show higher levels of aggression (Jin et al., 2023). In addition, experiences of social exclusion may activate hostile thoughts and hostile attribution, making individuals more likely to interpret ambiguous social information as hostile and thereby increasing aggressive tendencies. Negative emotions such as anger elicited by social exclusion may also further promote aggressive responses (DeWall et al., 2009; Shao and Zhang, 2021).

Social exclusion may also increase the likelihood of aggressive responses by altering individuals’ internal states. Relative deprivation refers to a subjective cognitive and emotional experience in which individuals perceive themselves to be disadvantaged through comparisons with relevant individuals or groups, which may further give rise to negative emotions such as anger and perceived unfairness (Pettigrew, 2016; Smith et al., 2012). Previous studies have found a significant positive association between social exclusion and relative deprivation (Duran Mucuk and Şahin, 2025). When individuals perceive themselves as being excluded from positive peer interactions or group belonging, they may become more aware of their relatively disadvantaged position through social comparison, thereby developing a sense of deprivation. Thus, social exclusion may serve as an important antecedent of relative deprivation. Relative deprivation may, in turn, be associated with aggressive behavior. Previous research has shown that individuals who perceive higher levels of deprivation are more likely to engage in aggressive behavior (Ding et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2023; Tong and Jiang, 2026). Within the framework of the General Aggression Model, relative deprivation can be viewed as an important internal state that may arise when individuals experience social exclusion as an adverse situation. As a negative emotional experience, relative deprivation is often accompanied by strong feelings of unfairness, anger, and resentment. When these feelings of deprivation accumulate, individuals may be more likely to use aggressive behavior as a means of compensation or emotional release. Therefore, relative deprivation may mediate the association between social exclusion and aggressive behavior.

In addition to influencing individuals’ internal psychological states, social exclusion may also indirectly increase the likelihood of aggressive behavior by changing adolescents’ patterns of peer affiliation. For adolescents, peer groups are an important source of social acceptance, belonging, and identity. Deviant peer affiliation refers to associations with peers who violate social norms and engage in similar activities and behaviors (Dishion and Tipsord, 2011). When adolescents repeatedly experience social exclusion, their needs for belonging and acceptance may remain unmet. This may encourage them to seek alternative peer relationships that provide recognition, acceptance, and a sense of belonging. Previous studies have shown that exclusion-related experiences, such as peer rejection and bullying victimization, are closely associated with deviant peer affiliation (Lansford et al., 2014; Rudolph et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2015; Dong et al., 2023). Social learning theory suggests that individuals can acquire and maintain behavioral patterns through observation, imitation, and social reinforcement (Akers, 2009; Dishion and Tipsord, 2011). Adolescents affiliated with deviant peers may be repeatedly exposed to aggressive behavior and related behavioral norms. Through observation and imitation, they may acquire similar behavioral patterns, which may be further reinforced by peer approval and support. This process may increase the likelihood of aggressive behavior (Lin et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024).

Notably, relative deprivation and deviant peer affiliation may not operate independently but may instead form a sequential process. Higher levels of relative deprivation indicate that individuals are more likely to perceive themselves as disadvantaged and to experience unfairness and negative emotions. These experiences may further increase their tendency to seek alternative sources of social support and group belonging. For some adolescents, deviant peer groups may be perceived as offering greater social status and autonomy (Tian et al., 2025). Such groups may also provide a certain degree of acceptance, recognition, and belonging, thereby serving as an important source of social connection (Williams, 2007). Therefore, adolescents with higher levels of relative deprivation may be more likely to affiliate with deviant peers to obtain the social status, support, and sense of belonging that are not fully satisfied in their existing relationships (Callan et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2021). A serial mediation analysis conducted among students in specialized schools found that relative deprivation was significantly and positively associated with deviant peer affiliation (Wang et al., 2026). Taken together, relative deprivation may further increase the likelihood of adolescents affiliating with deviant peers, and the two factors may form a serial mediating pathway between social exclusion and aggressive behavior.

In this study, students in specialized schools were defined as minors who, following an assessment and a formal decision, had been placed in these schools to receive specialized education because of serious misconduct. Given the characteristics of the study population and the limited number of specialized schools, purposive sampling was employed. Taking into account geographical distribution, schools’ willingness to participate, and the feasibility of data collection, three specialized schools located in Hunan, Shandong, and Hainan provinces, China, were selected. After the schools had been selected, all students who met the inclusion criteria were invited to participate. To facilitate centralized data collection and minimize disruption to normal teaching activities, the questionnaire survey was administered by class in accordance with the arrangements of each school. Based on the minimum sample size criterion of at least five participants per questionnaire item (Tinsley and Tinsley, 1987), the 43-item questionnaire used in this study required at least 215 valid participants. Allowing for an estimated 20% rate of invalid or incomplete responses, the target sample size was approximately 269 participants.

paras.sec_title: The Ostracism Experience Scale for Adolescents (OES-A)
paras.text: The OES-A was developed by Gilman et al. (2013) and subsequently adapted by Zhang et al. (2018). In the adaptation study, the OES-A demonstrated good structural validity among Chinese adolescents (χ2/df = 2.09, p < 0.001, CFI = 0.98, TLI = 0.98, and RMSEA = 0.04) and acceptable reliability (Cronbach’s α = 0.76; six-month test–retest reliability coefficient = 0.65). It consists of 11 items across two dimensions: neglect and rejection. Example items include “Other people often come to my home to play with me” and “When everyone is talking together, other people often ignore me.” Items are rated on a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (never) to 5 (always). Items in the rejection dimension are reverse-scored, such that higher total scores indicate higher levels of social exclusion. In the present study, the complete 11-item version was used, with no items omitted or modified. The scale demonstrated acceptable internal consistency in the current sample (Cronbach’s α = 0.76).

The present study used the RDQ developed by Ma (2012). It assesses individuals’ perceived disparity when comparing themselves with a reference group. It consists of four items. An example item is “Compared with the effort and work I have put in, my life should be better than it is now.” Items are rated on a 6-point Likert scale, with higher scores indicating higher levels of relative deprivation. The questionnaire has been used in studies involving Chinese adolescents, and previous research has supported its good structural validity (Wu and Zhang, 2024) and internal consistency (Kong et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2021). In the present study, the complete four-item version was used, with no items omitted or modified. The questionnaire demonstrated acceptable internal consistency in the current study (Cronbach’s α = 0.71).

The DPAQ adapted by Li et al. (2013) was used to assess deviant peer affiliation among students in specialized schools. It consists of eight items assessing deviant peer behaviors, such as truancy and drinking. Items are rated on a five-point Likert scale, with higher scores indicating higher levels of deviant peer affiliation. The questionnaire has demonstrated good structural validity (Wang et al., 2020) and internal consistency (Li et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026) among Chinese adolescents. No items were deleted or modified in the present study. In the current sample, the questionnaire demonstrated good internal consistency (Cronbach’s α = 0.80).

Aggressive behavior in adolescents was assessed using the revised BPAQ (Liu et al., 2009). The revision study reported good structural validity (KMO = 0.898, χ2 = 2886.45, df = 231, p < 0.01) and reliability (Cronbach’s α = 0.84, test–retest reliability = 0.92) among Chinese adolescents. It consists of 20 items across four dimensions: physical aggression, hostility, anger, and substitute aggression. Among them, physical aggression reflects aggressive behavioral manifestations, anger belongs to emotional expression, and hostility belongs to cognitive expression. Alternative aggression is manifested externally as causing harm to objects or indirectly attacking people or objects with words, and internally as suppressed negative emotions. An example item is “Some of my friends think I have a hot temper.” The scale uses a 5-point Likert format, with higher scores indicating greater levels of aggression. No items were deleted or modified in the present study. The scale demonstrated excellent internal consistency in the present study (Cronbach’s α = 0.91).

Data analyses were conducted using SPSS 31.0 and Mplus 8.3. First, descriptive statistics, correlation analyses, and Harman’s single-factor test were performed in SPSS 31.0. Harman’s single-factor test was used to assess potential common method bias (Zhou and Long, 2004). The results showed that 10 factors had eigenvalues greater than 1, and the first factor accounted for 20.00% of the total variance, which was below the recommended threshold of 40%. These results suggest that common method bias was unlikely to pose a serious threat to the validity of the findings. Second, a serial mediation model was tested in Mplus 8.3 to examine the mediating roles of relative deprivation and deviant peer affiliation in the association between social exclusion and aggressive behavior.

Descriptive statistics and correlations among the study variables are presented in Table 1. According to Cohen’s (1988) guidelines, social exclusion showed small positive correlations with relative deprivation (r = 0.13, p < 0.01), deviant peer affiliation (r = 0.18, p < 0.001), and aggressive behavior (r = 0.19, p < 0.001). Relative deprivation also showed small positive correlations with deviant peer affiliation (r = 0.23, p < 0.001) and aggressive behavior (r = 0.24, p < 0.001). In contrast, deviant peer affiliation was moderately and positively correlated with aggressive behavior (r = 0.42, p < 0.001).

paras.sec_title: The relationship between social exclusion and aggressive behavior
paras.text: The present study found that social exclusion was significantly and positively associated with aggressive behavior among specialized school students, thereby supporting Hypothesis 1. This finding is consistent with previous studies showing a positive association between social exclusion and aggressive behavior (Qiu et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025). One possible explanation is that social exclusion, as a typical negative life event, disrupts individuals’ emotional and cognitive processing. It may influence cognition, affect, and physiological arousal, thereby increasing the likelihood of aggressive responses (Allen et al., 2018). In addition, social exclusion can disrupt social connectedness and elicit “social pain” experiences that resemble physical pain, which may in turn activate hostile cognitions and aggressive tendencies among adolescents and elevate the risk of aggression (Bai and Yang, 2025; Mo et al., 2024). For students in specialized schools, who often have a history of problem behaviors and frequently come from left-behind, single-parent, or conflictual family environments, these experiences make them more likely to be ignored or marginalized in daily interactions, thereby intensifying experiences of social exclusion and further increasing the probability of aggressive behavior (Zhang and Li, 2025). Consequently, they are more likely to resort to aggressive behavior as a response to social exclusion.

paras.sec_title: The mediating role of relative deprivation
paras.text: Second, the present study found that relative deprivation mediated the association between social exclusion and aggressive behavior, supporting Hypothesis 2. This finding is consistent with previous studies (Yu et al., 2025). It suggests that social exclusion is associated with aggressive behavior not only directly but also indirectly through relative deprivation. Experiences of social exclusion among students in specialized schools may heighten their awareness of differences between themselves and others in social acceptance and group status. When these differences are perceived as signs of disadvantage or unfair treatment, stronger feelings of relative deprivation may arise. This finding is also consistent with the General Aggression Model. The negative cognitions and emotions involved in relative deprivation may further influence individuals’ appraisal of the current situation and the consequences of their behavior, thereby increasing the likelihood of aggressive behavior (Anderson and Bushman, 2002; Shao and Zhang, 2021). Therefore, when seeking to understand aggressive behavior among students in specialized schools, attention should be paid not only to their experiences of social exclusion but also to the relative deprivation that may arise from these experiences.

paras.sec_title: The mediating role of deviant peer affiliation
paras.text: In addition, the present study found that deviant peer affiliation mediated the association between social exclusion and aggressive behavior. Social exclusion involves various interpersonal threats and negative experiences. When adolescents repeatedly experience social exclusion, their needs for belonging and acceptance may not be fully satisfied. Under such circumstances, they may be more likely to seek alternative peer groups that can provide acceptance, recognition, and emotional support. Interactions with deviant peers often involve group-based activities, and repeated contact and shared activities may strengthen emotional bonds among group members. To some extent, these relationships may compensate for the unmet need for belonging resulting from social exclusion (Liu and Su, 2023; Yang and Huang, 2022). Therefore, individuals who experience higher levels of social exclusion may be more likely to affiliate with deviant peers. Previous studies have also shown that deviant peer affiliation is closely associated with aggressive behavior (Cairns et al., 1988; Lin et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2015). Through frequent interactions with deviant peers, adolescents may observe and imitate peers’ aggressive behavior and gradually acquire similar behavioral patterns. In addition, behavioral displays, peer pressure, and social reinforcement within peer interactions may further strengthen adolescents’ acceptance of deviant behavior and increase the likelihood of engaging in aggression (Dishion and Tipsord, 2011).

paras.sec_title: The mediating role of deviant peer affiliation
paras.text: Notably, among the two indirect pathways through relative deprivation and deviant peer affiliation, the indirect effect through deviant peer affiliation was larger. This difference in effect size may reflect the different processes represented by the two mediators. Relative deprivation mainly reflects the internal cognitive and emotional processes that follow experiences of social exclusion (Smith et al., 2012), whereas deviant peer affiliation involves more sustained peer interaction and social reinforcement processes (Dishion and Tipsord, 2011). Therefore, when understanding the association between social exclusion and aggressive behavior among students in specialized schools, deviant peer affiliation may represent a particularly important social factor.

paras.sec_title: Serial mediation of relative deprivation and deviant peer affiliation
paras.text: The present study also identified a serial mediating pathway through relative deprivation and deviant peer affiliation between social exclusion and aggressive behavior, supporting Hypothesis 4. This finding suggests that the relative deprivation associated with social exclusion may not remain only at the level of adolescents’ internal experiences but may also extend to their peer relationships. When adolescents experience higher levels of relative deprivation, they may perceive greater psychological stress, lower social status, and stronger feelings of unfairness (Tian et al., 2025). As a result, they may seek affiliation with deviant peers as a way to relieve psychological tension. Adolescents with higher levels of relative deprivation may therefore be more likely to affiliate with deviant peers who are subject to fewer behavioral constraints and are perceived as having greater autonomy and social status (Callan et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2021). Overall, these findings suggest that the association between social exclusion and aggressive behavior may involve a process that extends from internal psychological experiences to external peer relationships, providing a more integrated explanation of aggressive behavior among students in specialized schools.

At the school level, three complementary strategies may be considered. First, schools should foster an inclusive and supportive social environment. Positive teacher–student relationships and peer interactions can strengthen adolescents’ sense of school belonging (Allen et al., 2022). Therefore, schools may foster supportive teacher–student relationships and provide opportunities for cooperative activities and peer support to promote positive interpersonal interactions and mitigate the negative effects associated with experiences of social exclusion. Second, interventions should strengthen students’ cognitive reappraisal and emotion-regulation skills. School-based emotion-regulation interventions have been shown to improve adolescents’ emotion-regulation skills and psychological adjustment (Pedrini et al., 2022). Accordingly, cognitive reappraisal and emotion-regulation strategies may be incorporated into intervention programs to help students interpret negative interpersonal experiences more adaptively and regulate negative emotions associated with perceived unfairness, anger, and resentment, thereby potentially reducing the likelihood of aggressive behavior. Finally, schools should promote positive and supportive peer relationships. Prosocial and deviant peer affiliations may have different implications for adolescent adjustment and behavior (Yoon et al., 2025). Therefore, schools may provide more opportunities for prosocial peer interactions and incorporate social skills training and guidance on peer relationships to help students develop stable and supportive peer relationships and reduce the potential negative influence of deviant peer affiliation.
